name: Dull Green
lede: Dull Green is a plain descriptive name for a mid green of low saturation, and as a painters' word it means a green with its chroma turned down.

sections.title: What the swatch is
sections.body:
The swatch is #74A662, a mid green that sits in ISCC-NBS block 148 and also appears in the xkcd survey [1]. Its nearest named neighbor is [[asparagus]], and [[moss]] is 7.5 units away [1]. It is a yellowish green with chroma of about 42, which is middling, so the screen color is softer than a leaf green but far from grey [1].

"Dull" is a description, not a historical name, so the books attach it to other things [2][3]. The label was never a single color.

sections.title: How the books use the word
sections.body:
Gurney uses dull greens to mean the lower-chroma end of a painter's gamut: a palette with strong cyan and magenta but weaker yellows, violets and dull greens [2]. Gage notes the violets, yellows and dull greens in a 1911 patchwork coverlet Sonia Delaunay made for her baby [3].

In Paterson, *lovat* is a dull green named for a Scottish town and used of tweed cloth, spelled Lovatt at first [4]. Salter, quoted in the Pigment Compendium, called uranium green a dull olive-leaning oxide, almost black in lumps, and the Compendium thinks artists rarely if ever used it [5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 16 works [6]. The top two are the *Portrait of Emperor Jahangir* [[painting:aic-62243|Portrait of Emperor Jahangir]] at 51 per cent and a Sérusier landscape at 36 [6]. A Van Gogh painting, [[painting:nga-163323|Green Wheat Fields, Auvers]], follows [6]. Van Gogh has three of his 49 works here, a rate 91 times the archive's [6].

France supplies eight hits, 3.5 times its share [6]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so the color is a screen color [6]. In Google Books *dull green* is present from 1800 and peaks about 1926 [7].
